February 6
Epiphany 5C — The Fifth Sunday of Epiphany
Colors: green
Judg 6:11-24
Psalm 85
1 Cor 15:1-11
Lk 5:1-11
To the Saints at Vanadium Woods,
February 6, 2022
Grace and peace from our Lord Jesus Christ, the son of our Father in Heaven, who knows us and trusts us.


The Old Testament lesson today is the beginning of the Story of Gideon (Judges 6:11-24). The thing most people know about Gideon is that he is the namesake of the folks who put Bibles in motel rooms. Sadly, the story does not carry through on the following Sundays and the beginning of the story makes little sense unless you can get through to the end.


The backdrop of the story is: The Midianites have been raiding Israel for a number of years, hauling off cattle and harvest. The people of Israel cry out to the Lord because of the Midianites. A prophet of the Lord responds to the cries of the people by saying, basically, "It's your own fault for worshiping other gods."


Even so, the Lord hears the cry of His people and appoints a leader. That leader would be Gideon. Here lies an important point: In spite of the people of Israel worshiping other gods, the Lord is still intent on saving them. If you take nothing else home today, take this: It is the intention of Our Father in Heaven to deliver us from our failings and rebellion against Him.


The story begins with Gideon hiding from the Midianites while beating out wheat in a winepress. While he works, an angel of the Lord comes to him saying, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.”


I found this particular saying of the angel perplexing. It breaks the pattern of angels whose first words are usually, "be not afraid." I can only conclude that Gideon does not immediately recognize this angel as an angel. The other perplexing thing is the angel sounds sarcastic, at least to my ear. After all, Gideon is hiding from the Midianites rather than confronting them. Furthermore, if we continue to follow the story, we find Gideon was pretty much afraid to do what the Lord had called him to do. In total, Gideon asks for 4 different signs from the Lord. By most metrics, Gideon does not sound valiant or faithful.


That being said, neither the Lord nor angels come across as sarcastic types. Additionally, in spite of Gideon's reluctance to take on the task God has given him, the author of Hebrews in the New Testament refers to Gideon as one of the heroes of the Old Testament (see Hebrew 11:32). 


If the author of Hebrews thinks Gideon is a mighty man of valor, and the angel of the Lord thinks Gideon is a mighty man of valor, and Gideon does not look like a mighty man of valor, what then is going on?


Eventually, Gideon does lead a scant 300 men - reduced by the Lord from 32000 - into battle, doing exactly what the Lord wants him to do.


My conclusion is: what I initially thought was sarcasm turns out to be a prophecy of a sort. "Of a sort" because most prophecies talk about what will happen off in the future and the angel of the Lord speaks as if Gideon were already a mighty man of valor. The angel of the Lord appears to know something about Gideon that Gideon does not know about himself.


This all gets even more confusing as the author of Judges switches back and forth between calling the other person in the story, "the angel of the Lord"  and "the Lord". Since the angel of the Lord does not act or sound like other angels presented to us in Scripture (and remembering some things taught in seminary), I hesitantly conclude the person speaking with Gideon is actually the Word of the Lord - that is, the preincarnate Jesus.


If I am correct, and I think I am, or I wouldn't say it, what we have is the Word of the Lord, knowing something about Gideon that is not immediately obvious to us. To my ear, this does sound like the kind of thing Jesus would say in the New Testament. Even so, that is hardly the point. The point is what is not obvious to us is obvious to the Lord. The Lord knows Gideon to be a mighty man of valor even when we - or Gideon - can't see it. The Lord sees things differently than we do. When I read Scripture and come across the Lord using His special insight when calling the people he does, I find myself thinking things like, "There goes that crazy Lord, doing the unexpected again." I've come to expect the unexpected from the Lord.


Well, that's in Scripture and we don't live in Scripture. We would like to have a way to apply what we are told here and now. Actually, I think most people would like to be told that this lesson shows us how much God wants us to be healthy, and wealthy. No where in Scripture is that sort of lesson taught (possibly surprising many a media evangelist).


What is taught in Scripture is the Lord sees us and judges us very differently than we do. The Lord knows Gideon to be the mighty man of valor needed for the task at hand even when no one else can see the evidence. What we conclude is: When the Lord calls us to a task, even when we and everyone else are inclined to say, "There goes that crazy Lord again, mixing me up with someone else," know this: you are wrong.


Of course, not many of us are called to drive out the Midianites, or lead the chosen people out of Egypt, or become king, all these seem like huge tasks in our eyes. On the other hand there are simple things, things like welcoming the stranger, visiting the sick, feeding the hungry, being merciful, all done on a small scale; they seem small in our eyes, but they are not.


Jesus tells us that the weightier matters of the Law are justice, mercy, and trusting the Lord (Matthew 23:23). When these are practiced as we are all called to practice them, the seemingly huge tasks of faith, like driving out the Midianites, simply become unnecessary. We are the people of justice, mercy, and trusting the Lord. That is our calling, and that is our task.


The peace of God, which passes all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in the knowledge and love of God, and of His Son Jesus Christ our Lord; and the blessing of God Almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, be among you, and remain with you always.
